                <p>
                    Imagine you're watching water swirl down a drain, or smoke curling from a candle. How does it move? Why does it behave the way it does? These are questions that the Navier-Stokes equations try to answer. They're the mathematical rulebook for predicting how all fluids move — water, air, blood, everything!
                </p>

                <svg width="100%" viewBox="0 0 680 380" style="background: linear-gradient(135deg, rgba(102, 126, 234, 0.1) 0%, rgba(118, 75, 162, 0.05) 100%); border-radius: 12px; padding: 20px; margin: 20px 0; border: 1px solid rgba(102, 126, 234, 0.2);">
                    <!-- Title -->

                    <!-- Inward Spiral Box -->
                    <rect x="40" y="60" width="280" height="300" rx="12" fill="rgba(102, 126, 234, 0.1)" stroke="rgba(102, 126, 234, 0.3)" stroke-width="2"/>
                    <text x="180" y="85" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size: 14px; font-weight: 700; fill: #a8b5ff;">Inward Spiral</text>

                    <text x="60" y="135" style="font-size: 11px; fill: #d0d0e0;">Fluid moves in circular</text>
                    <text x="60" y="152" style="font-size: 11px; fill: #d0d0e0;">patterns, spiraling toward</text>
                    <text x="60" y="169" style="font-size: 11px; fill: #d0d0e0;">the center axis</text>

                    <line x1="60" y1="185" x2="300" y2="185" stroke="rgba(102, 126, 234, 0.2)" stroke-width="1"/>

                    <text x="60" y="205" style="font-size: 12px; fill: #a8b5ff; font-weight: 600;">In Navier-Stokes Terms:</text>
                    <text x="60" y="225" style="font-size: 11px; fill: #d0d0e0;">This is the (u·∇)u term</text>
                    <text x="60" y="242" style="font-size: 11px; fill: #d0d0e0;">"Convection" - how the</text>
                    <text x="60" y="259" style="font-size: 11px; fill: #d0d0e0;">fluid's own motion</text>
                    <text x="60" y="276" style="font-size: 11px; fill: #d0d0e0;">affects its acceleration</text>

                    <text x="60" y="305" style="font-size: 12px; fill: #81c784; font-weight: 600;">The Danger:</text>
                    <text x="60" y="325" style="font-size: 11px; fill: #ffb74d;">As spiral tightens,</text>
                    <text x="60" y="342" style="font-size: 11px; fill: #ffb74d;">velocity INCREASES</text>

                    <rect x="360" y="60" width="280" height="300" rx="12" fill="rgba(76, 175, 80, 0.1)" stroke="rgba(76, 175, 80, 0.3)" stroke-width="2"/>

                    <text x="380" y="115" style="font-size: 12px; fill: #d0d0e0; font-weight: 600;">What's Happening:</text>
                    <text x="380" y="135" style="font-size: 11px; fill: #d0d0e0;">Fluid is stretched</text>
                    <text x="380" y="152" style="font-size: 11px; fill: #d0d0e0;">vertically while spiraling</text>
                    <text x="380" y="169" style="font-size: 11px; fill: #d0d0e0;">inward (two forces)</text>

                    <line x1="380" y1="185" x2="620" y2="185" stroke="rgba(76, 175, 80, 0.2)" stroke-width="1"/>

                    <text x="380" y="205" style="font-size: 12px; fill: #81c784; font-weight: 600;">In Navier-Stokes Terms:</text>
                    <text x="380" y="225" style="font-size: 11px; fill: #d0d0e0;">This involves ∂u/∂t</text>
                    <text x="380" y="242" style="font-size: 11px; fill: #d0d0e0;">(acceleration over time)</text>
                    <text x="380" y="259" style="font-size: 11px; fill: #d0d0e0;">and ∇²u (viscosity effects)</text>
                    <text x="380" y="276" style="font-size: 11px; fill: #d0d0e0;">working together</text>

                    <text x="380" y="305" style="font-size: 12px; fill: #81c784; font-weight: 600;">The Danger:</text>
                    <text x="380" y="325" style="font-size: 11px; fill: #ffb74d;">Can stretching + spiraling</text>
                    <text x="380" y="342" style="font-size: 11px; fill: #ffb74d;">cause infinite velocity?</text>

                <h3>The Problem That Nobody Solved</h3>
                <p>
                    For 90 years, mathematicians asked: Can these equations ever reach a point where they become impossible to calculate? Specifically, can fluid velocity become infinite (impossible in real life)?
                </p>

                <p>
                    This question is SO important that the Clay Mathematics Institute offered <strong>$1 million</strong> to whoever solved it. It's been one of the top unsolved problems in mathematics.
                </p>

                <h3>Two Possible Answers</h3>
                <p>
                    Scientists wondered: Is it possible that at some point in time, the equations say "velocity = infinity"? Or do they always stay reasonable?
                </p>

                <ul>
                    <li><strong>Option A (Hope):</strong> Equations always work. Fluids behave predictably forever.</li>
                    <li><strong>Option B (Scary):</strong> Equations can break. At some point, they might become impossible to solve.</li>
                </ul>

                <h3>Real-World Examples</h3>
                <p>
                    These equations are used to predict:
                </p>

                <div class="benefit-card">
                    <strong>🌪️ Weather</strong> — Storms, hurricanes, wind patterns
                </div>

                <div class="benefit-card">

                <h3>The Historic Announcement</h3>
                <p>
                    On September 8, 2026, OpenAI announced something extraordinary: An artificial intelligence system solved one of the Clay Mathematics Institute's Millennium Prize Problems. After 90 years of unsolved mystery, AI cracked it in just 88 hours.
                </p>

                <div class="highlight-box success">
                    <strong>✅ What They Proved:</strong> The Navier-Stokes equations CAN develop a singularity under certain conditions. In other words: Yes, the equations can reach a breaking point.
                </div>

                <div class="highlight-box success">
                    <strong>📅 Timeline Status (as of September 25, 2026):</strong> This breakthrough was announced on September 8, 2026 — 17 days ago. Verification by the Clay Mathematics Institute is ongoing.
                </div>

                <h3>How Did AI Solve It?</h3>
                <p>
                    It wasn't a single AI. OpenAI used approximately 10,000 autonomous AI agents working together for 88 hours. These agents:
                </p>

                <ul>
                    <li>Tried millions of different combinations</li>
                    <li>Searched for patterns and solutions</li>
                    <li>Built on mathematical frameworks from human researchers</li>
                    <li>Finally found proof of singularities</li>
                </ul>

                <p>
                    The cost? Several million dollars in computing power.
                </p>

                <h3>What's the Exact Finding?</h3>
                <p>
                    OpenAI proved that when a fluid is pushed by external forces (like wind or a pump), the equations CAN develop a singularity — meaning velocity becomes infinite and the math breaks.
                </p>

                <div class="highlight-box">
                    <strong>Important Note:</strong> This is only for fluids with external forces. The question of whether fluids naturally break down on their own is still unsolved!
                </div>

                    <li>Design 30-40% more efficient wind turbines</li>
                    <li>Optimize water flow in dams</li>
                    <li>Make solar thermal systems more powerful</li>
                </ul>

                <div class="benefit-card">
                    <strong>Real impact:</strong> Cheaper renewable energy → lower electricity bills, faster transition to clean energy.
                </div>

                <h3>🚗 Better Car & Motorcycle Design</h3>
                <p>
                    <strong>Current problem:</strong> Racing teams and engineers have to guess about air flow around vehicles.
                </p>

                <p>
                    <strong>With this breakthrough:</strong> Cars can be:
                </p>

                <ul>
                    <li>More aerodynamic (faster, sleeker)</li>
                    <li>More fuel-efficient</li>
                    <li>Safer in high-speed maneuvers</li>
                </ul>

                <h3>🌊 Better Understand Oceans</h3>
                <p>
                    <strong>Current problem:</strong> Ocean currents and tsunamis are hard to predict accurately.
                </p>

                <p>
                    <strong>With this breakthrough:</strong> Scientists can:
                </p>

                <ul>
                    <li>Better predict tsunami waves</li>
                    <li>Understand ocean currents for shipping</li>
                    <li>Predict algae blooms and marine pollution spread</li>
                </ul>

                <p>

                </p>

                    <li><strong>2-5 years:</strong> New aircraft designs, improved medical devices</li>
                    <li><strong>5-10 years:</strong> Noticeable improvements in wind turbines, lower energy costs</li>

            <article class="blog-post" id="blog-3">
                <h2>The Controversy: Did OpenAI Get All the Credit?</h2>
                <p class="date">September 25, 2026</p>
                <span class="tag">Controversy</span>
                <span class="tag">Ethics</span>

                <h3>Not Everyone is Celebrating</h3>
                <p>
                    While OpenAI celebrated their breakthrough, mathematicians raised questions: "Wait... did you actually solve this alone? What about the researchers who started this work?"
                </p>

                <h3>The Credit Dispute: Verified Timeline</h3>
                <p>
                    Here's what actually happened (with verified dates):
                </p>

                <div class="benefit-card">
                    <strong>October 2024 - February 2025</strong><br/>
                    Researchers Diego Córdoba and Luis Martínez-Zoroa published foundational framework for finding singularities. Their preprint: first submitted October 2024, revised February 2025.
                </div>

                <div class="benefit-card">
                    <strong>September 1, 2026 (2 days before announcement)</strong><br/>
                    OpenAI heard rumors that rival company Anthropic was close to solving two Millennium Prize problems. OpenAI immediately launched their internal model at the remaining problems.
                </div>

                <div class="benefit-card">
                    <strong>September 1-8, 2026 (88 hours of computation)</strong><br/>
                    OpenAI ran ~10,000 AI agents working on the existing mathematical framework. Cost: multiple millions of dollars in computing resources.
                </div>

                <div class="benefit-card">
                    <strong>Tuesday, September 8, 2026 (17 days ago)</strong><br/>
                    OpenAI publicly announces to media: "Our AI solves Navier-Stokes!" Formal proof checked in Lean programming language.
                </div>

                <div class="benefit-card">
                    <strong>September 8-25, 2026 (Current period - 17 days)</strong><br/>
                    Mathematicians raise credit concerns. Clay Mathematics Institute begins formal verification. No official prize awarded yet.
                </div>

                <h3>A Simple Analogy</h3>
                <p>
                    Think of it like homework:
                </p>

                <ul>
                    <li><strong>Student A:</strong> Studies for 3 months, writes detailed notes</li>
                    <li><strong>Student B:</strong> Reads Student A's notes, uses an AI app to finish the last 20%, then tells the teacher: "I solved it!"</li>
                    <li><strong>Student A:</strong> "Um... hello? That's my work!"</li>
                </ul>

                <h3>What Mathematicians Said</h3>
                <p>
                    Some concerns raised:
                </p>

                <div class="benefit-card">
                    <strong>Concern 1:</strong> "OpenAI didn't credit earlier researchers properly"
                </div>

                <div class="benefit-card">
                    <strong>Concern 2:</strong> "Is this really 'AI solving it' or just 'AI completing human work'?"
                </div>

                <div class="benefit-card">
                    <strong>Concern 3:</strong> "Why the rush? Was this about science or corporate competition?"
                </div>

                <div class="benefit-card">
                    <strong>Concern 4:</strong> "They spent millions of dollars. Is this fair competition?"
                </div>

                <h3>The Bigger Question</h3>
                <p>
                    This raises an important question about AI breakthroughs: When AI solves something using existing research, who gets credit?
                </p>

                <ul>
                    <li>The AI company that ran the computation?</li>
                    <li>The researchers who created the framework?</li>
                    <li>Both together?</li>
                </ul>

                <p>
                    There's no clear answer yet, and that's part of the controversy.
                </p>

                <h3>OpenAI's Response</h3>
                <p>
                    OpenAI said they improved on the earlier research and mentioned the previous work, but many felt the initial announcement didn't emphasize this enough.
                </p>

                <h3>The $1 Million Question</h3>
                <p>
                    <strong>Will OpenAI get the prize money?</strong>
                </p>

                <p>
                    The Clay Mathematics Institute is still verifying the proof. They might:
                </p>

                <ul>
                    <li>Award the full $1 million to OpenAI</li>
                    <li>Ask OpenAI to share the prize with earlier researchers</li>
                    <li>Require better credit attribution</li>
                </ul>

                <p>
                    Nobody knows yet!
                </p>

                <h3>What This Means Going Forward</h3>
                <p>
                    This controversy highlights an important issue: As AI becomes better at solving scientific problems, we need better rules about credit and proper attribution. It's not just about fairness — it's about how science should work.
                </p>

                <div class="highlight-box">
                    <strong>Key takeaway:</strong> Great discoveries require standing on the shoulders of giants. Proper credit to everyone involved makes science stronger.

    <script>
        function showBlog(index) {
            const posts = document.querySelectorAll('.blog-post');
            const buttons = document.querySelectorAll('.nav-btn');

            posts.forEach(post => post.classList.remove('active'));
            buttons.forEach(btn => btn.classList.remove('active'));

            posts[index].classList.add('active');
            buttons[index].classList.add('active');

            window.scrollTo({ top: 0, behavior: 'smooth' });
        }
    </script>
